summary: Blockchain is a decentralized, immutable ledger that stores data in blocks linked by cryptography, best known for underpinning cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin but with broader applications across industries. It works by distributing copies across a network, using cryptographic hashing and consensus mechanisms like proof-of-work to secure transactions, offering transparency and security while facing challenges such as scalability and energy consumption.

claims.text: Blockchain is a type of shared database that stores data in blocks linked together via cryptography.
claims.evidence_quote: Blockchain is a type of shared database that differs from a typical database in the way it stores information; blockchains store data in blocks linked together via cryptography.

claims.text: The Bitcoin blockchain collects transaction information into 4MB files called blocks.
claims.evidence_quote: The Bitcoin blockchain collects transaction information and enters it into a 4MB file called a block

claims.text: Bitcoin's proof-of-work system consumes more energy than Finland.
claims.evidence_quote: the energy consumed by the millions of devices on the Bitcoin network is more than what Finland uses

claims.text: Bitcoin confirmation takes about one hour because it averages just under 10 minutes per block and requires six confirmations.
claims.evidence_quote: Confirmation takes about one hour to complete because it averages just under 10 minutes per block (the first block with your transaction and five following blocks multiplied by 10 equals 60 minutes).

claims.text: The Bitcoin network hashed at a rate of around 850 exahashes per second as of May 12, 2026.
claims.evidence_quote: the Bitcoin network hashed at a rate of around 850 exahashes per second as of May 12, 2026.

claims.text: As of May 12, 2026, approximately 39.06 million ETH were staked by more than one million validators on Ethereum.
claims.evidence_quote: As of May 12, 2026, approximately 39.06 million ETH were staked by more than one million validators.

claims.text: Blockchain technology was first outlined in 1991 by Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta.
claims.evidence_quote: Blockchain technology was first outlined in 1991 by Stuart Haber and W. Scott Stornetta, two researchers who wanted to implement a system where document timestamps couldn't be tampered with.

claims.text: Bitcoin was launched in January 2009, giving blockchain its first real-world application.
claims.evidence_quote: it wasn’t until almost two decades later, with the launch of Bitcoin in January 2009, that blockchain had its first real-world application.

claims.text: Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, described it as 'a new electronic cash system that’s fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.'
claims.evidence_quote: a new electronic cash system that’s fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.

claims.text: Blockchain can be used to immutably record votes in an election, product inventories, state identifications, deeds to homes, and much more.
claims.evidence_quote: Blockchain can be used to immutably record any number of data points. The data can be transactions, votes in an election, product inventories, state identifications, deeds to homes, and much more.

claims.text: IBM's Food Trust blockchain can trace the journey of food products through the supply chain, showing their point of origin and the path between suppliers.
claims.evidence_quote: IBM's Food Trust blockchain can trace the journey of food products through the supply chain, showing their point of origin and the path between suppliers.

claims.text: Blockchain can process transactions in minutes or seconds, regardless of holidays or time of day, unlike banks that operate only during business hours.
claims.evidence_quote: By integrating blockchain into banks, consumers might see their transactions processed in minutes or seconds—the time it takes to add a block to the blockchain, regardless of holidays or the time of day or week.

claims.text: Blockchain can eliminate the need for third-party verification, reducing costs associated with banks and notaries.
claims.evidence_quote: Blockchain eliminates the need for third-party verification—and, with it, their associated costs.

claims.text: Bitcoin's blockchain can only manage an estimated seven transactions per second (TPS), while Visa can process 1,700 TPS.
claims.evidence_quote: it's estimated that the blockchain network can only manage an estimated seven transactions per second (TPS). ... Legacy brand Visa, for context, can process 1,700 TPS.

claims.text: The Silk Road, an online dark web marketplace for illegal drugs and money laundering, ran between January 2011 and October 2013 when the FBI shut it down.
claims.evidence_quote: The most cited example of blockchain being used for illicit transactions is probably the Silk Road, an online dark web illegal-drug and money laundering marketplace that ran between January 2011 and October 2013, when the FBI shut it down.

claims.text: As of 2026, 47% of Americans say they will never purchase a cryptocurrency.
claims.evidence_quote: As of 2026, 47% of Americans still say they will never purchase a cryptocurrency.

claims.text: According to The World Bank, as of 2024 data, an estimated 1.3 billion adults don't have bank accounts or any means of storing their money or wealth.
claims.evidence_quote: According to The World Bank, as of 2024 data, an estimated 1.3 billion adults don't have bank accounts or any means of storing their money or wealth.

claims.text: Blockchain transactions are pseudonymous, not fully anonymous, because there is a viewable address that can be associated with a user if the information gets out.
claims.evidence_quote: It is a common misconception that blockchain networks like Bitcoin are fully anonymous; they are actually pseudonymous because there is a viewable address that can be associated with a user if the information gets out.

claims.text: A 51% attack on Bitcoin is nearly impossible because the attacker would need at least half of the network's computational power.
claims.evidence_quote: the attacker would need at least half of the network's computational power (a 51% attack). On the Bitcoin and other larger blockchains, this is nearly impossible.

claims.text: Blockchain can provide a way to secure personal information for citizens of countries with unstable or underdeveloped governments.
claims.evidence_quote: Provides a banking alternative and a way to secure personal information for citizens of countries with unstable or underdeveloped governments.
